source: Herbs in Pregnancy and Lactation — Eric Yarnell, ND (2022, last updated 20 October 2023)
caveat: All listings are Dr Eric Yarnell's opinion only. This information is meant for medical professionals, is not a substitute for individualised medical care, and is not specific advice for any patient. Consult the medical literature before making any decision about herb use in pregnancy or lactation — new information can appear at any time. In many cases the benefits may outweigh the risks of using herbs short term where an illness would otherwise damage or threaten a pregnancy. Herbs should be used for the least time necessary at the lowest dose possible in pregnancy, with the exception of a handful of pregnancy tonics. A rating of “safe” does not mean harm is impossible, only that it is not documented and, if it happens, is extremely rare. Information about one form or part of a herb may not apply to all forms or parts of that herb.
sources: Mills S, Bone K. The Essential Guide to Herbal Safety, 1st ed. Churchill Livingstone, 2005 — pregnancy and lactation categories.
Mills E, Dugoua JJ, Perri D, Koren G. Herbal Medicines in Pregnancy and Lactation: An Evidence-Based Approach. Taylor and Francis, 2006 — evidence levels.
Brinker F. Herb Contraindications and Drug Interactions, 3rd ed., 2001, Appendix C2 — lactation codes.
American Herbal Products Association. Botanical Safety Handbook, 2nd ed. Gardner Z, McGuffin M (eds). CRC Press, 2013 — safety classes.

levels.avoid: Contraindicated, or rated D/X in pregnancy, SD/X in lactation, or AHPA class 2b/2c.
levels.caution: Use with caution — a C rating, an AHPA class 3, a Brinker lactation code, or a theoretical concern.
levels.evidence: Rated in the A–B range with no contraindication recorded.
levels.unrated: No rating in any of the four sources; the notes may still carry information.
